title: Reduced effective resolution from attention averaging
description: Self-attention reduces the number of operations to constant between any two positions, but at the cost of reduced effective resolution because attention weights are averaged over positions. Multi-Head Attention is used to counteract this effect.
canonical_description: self-attention reduces effective resolution by averaging attention-weighted positions

evidence.anchor: reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions
evidence.quote: In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section~[REF:sec:attention].

verdict.reasoning: Paper 4 (CSP) directly addresses the gap by replacing softmax-based multi-head attention with hard permutation matrices, which eliminates the averaging-over-positions issue entirely for doubly-stochastic (bidirectional) attention. It proves theoretically that CSP avoids the rank/variance collapse caused by averaging. However, the authors explicitly note that CSP cannot be applied to causal/decoder attention (where attention maps are lower-triangular), so the effective-resolution problem from averaging in generative Transformers remains open. The other four papers study related but distinct phenomena (depth-wise rank collapse, head-channel non-identifiability, spectral properties of weight matrices, kernel SVD reformulation) and do not engage with the positional-averaging / effective-resolution problem at all. Thus, the gap is partially solved: solved for bidirectional attention, open for causal attention.

paper.title: Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth
paper.abstract: Attention-based architectures have become ubiquitous in machine learning, yet our understanding of the reasons for their effectiveness remains limited. This work proposes a new way to understand self-attention networks: we show that their output can be decomposed into a sum of smaller terms, each involving the operation of a sequence of attention heads across layers. Using this decomposition, we prove that self-attention possesses a strong inductive bias towards "token uniformity". Specifically, without skip connections or multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), the output converges doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix. On the other hand, skip connections and MLPs stop the output from degeneration. Our experiments verify the identified convergence phenomena on different variants of standard transformer architectures.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper studies rank collapse in deep self-attention networks, proving that the output of a pure self-attention network (without skip connections or MLPs) converges doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix (all tokens identical) with depth. It develops a path decomposition to analyze multi-head attention networks and shows that skip connections and MLPs counteract this depth-wise rank collapse. The paper does not address the per-layer reduction in effective resolution caused by attention averaging over positions, nor does it study how Multi-Head Attention counteracts such resolution loss.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the per-layer reduction in effective resolution because attention weights average over positions (a single attention head produces a weighted average of value vectors, smoothing out token distinctions), and the claim that Multi-Head Attention counteracts this effect. This paper does not address this problem at all. It studies a different phenomenon — depth-wise rank collapse (the output converging to a rank-1 matrix as layers increase) — and finds that more attention heads actually accelerate rank collapse (Theorem 2.3 includes a factor of H in the numerator of the convergence bound), which is the opposite of what the gap claims about Multi-Head Attention counteracting resolution loss. The gap's specific problem remains entirely unaddressed.

paper.title: Rank, Head-Channel Non-Identifiability, and Symmetry Breaking: A Precise Analysis of Representational Collapse in Transformers
paper.abstract: A widely cited result by Dong et al. (2021) showed that Transformers built from self-attention alone, without skip connections or feed-forward layers, suffer from rapid rank collapse: all token representations converge to a single direction. The proposed remedy was the MLP. We show that this picture, while correct in the regime studied by Dong, is incomplete in ways that matter for architectural understanding. Three results are established. First, layer normalisation is precisely affine-rank-neutral: it preserves the affine rank of the token representation set exactly. The widespread claim that LN "plays no role" is imprecise; the correct statement is sharper. Second, residual connections generically obstruct rank collapse in real Transformers such as BERT-base, in a measure-theoretic sense, without contribution from the MLP. The MLP's irreplaceable function is different: generating feature directions outside the linear span of the original token embeddings, which no stack of attention layers can produce. Third, a phenomenon distinct from rank collapse is identified: head-channel non-identifiability. After multi-head attention sums per-head outputs through the output projection, individual contributions cannot be canonically attributed to a specific head; n(H-1)d_k degrees of freedom per layer remain ambiguous when recovering a single head from the mixed signal. The MLP cannot remedy this because it acts on the post-summation signal. A constructive partial remedy is proposed: a position-gated output projection (PG-OP) at parameter overhead below 1.6% of the standard output projection. The four collapse phenomena identified in the literature -- rank collapse in depth, in width, head-channel non-identifiability, and entropy collapse -- are unified under a symmetry-breaking framework, each corresponding to a distinct symmetry of the Transformer's forward pass.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper studies rank collapse (token representations converging to a single direction) and head-channel non-identifiability (per-head contributions becoming irrecoverable after summation in multi-head attention). It proves that layer normalization is rank-neutral, residual connections generically obstruct rank collapse, and identifies head-channel non-identifiability as a distinct phenomenon from rank collapse. It also proposes a symmetry-breaking framework and a position-gated output projection as a partial remedy.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific gap of "reduced effective resolution from attention averaging" — the phenomenon where self-attention's weighted averaging over positions reduces the model's ability to distinguish fine-grained patterns, which Multi-Head Attention is designed to counteract. The paper's focus on rank collapse (all tokens becoming identical) and head-channel non-identifiability (losing per-head attribution after summation) are distinct phenomena from effective resolution loss due to positional averaging. The gap remains entirely open.

paper.title: A Random Matrix Theory Perspective on the Learning Dynamics of Multi-head Latent Attention
paper.abstract: In this work, we study how multi-head latent attention (MLA), a popular strategy for compressing key/value memory, affects a transformer's internal capacity during pretraining. Using a lightweight suite of Marchenko-Pastur (MP) diagnostics, we analyze the spectrum of the $W_{Q}W_{K}^\top$ gram matrix throughout training, comparing three variants: the standard multi-head attention (MHA) baseline, MLA-PreRoPE with rotary applied before compression, and MLA-Decoupled, which shares a single rotary sub-vector across all heads. Our random matrix analysis reveals \textbf{three key findings:} \textbf{ i)} capacity bottlenecks emerge locally: both MHA and MLA-PreRoPE exhibit sharp, early spikes in specific layers that persist and propagate, disrupting the balance between bulk and outlier directions; \textbf{ ii)} these spikes coincide with rank collapse, concentrating the model's expressivity into narrow subspaces; \textbf{ iii)} only the decoupled variant prevents this cascade, maintaining broad spectral support and suppressing outlier formation across layers. These results underscore that \emph{how} rotary embeddings are applied is just as critical as \emph{where} compression occurs. Sharing rotary components across heads mitigates spectral fragmentation and preserves representational capacity.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper studies the spectral dynamics (eigenvalue distribution) of the W_Q W_K^T Gram matrix in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) variants using Random Matrix Theory. It finds that different MLA configurations produce different spectral spike patterns, with the decoupled variant (sharing rotary embeddings across heads) suppressing outliers and preserving stable rank better than standard MHA or Pre-RoPE MLA. The work focuses on spectral properties of weight matrices and rank collapse under latent compression.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns "reduced effective resolution from attention averaging" — the problem that self-attention averages attention weights over positions, reducing the model's ability to distinguish between different positions, which Multi-Head Attention is meant to counteract. This paper does not study attention weight distributions over positions, positional resolution, or the averaging behavior of attention weights. It studies spectral properties of the query-key weight Gram matrix (W_Q W_K^T), which is a different notion of "effective rank" related to weight matrix singular values, not the positional resolution of attention distributions. The specific problem of how attention averaging over positions reduces effective resolution, and how multi-head architectures counteract this, remains entirely unaddressed.

paper.title: Towards Better Multi-head Attention via Channel-wise Sample Permutation
paper.abstract: Transformer plays a central role in many fundamental deep learning models, e.g., the ViT in computer vision and the BERT and GPT in natural language processing, whose effectiveness is mainly attributed to its multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism. In this study, we propose a simple and novel channel-wise sample permutation (CSP) operator, achieving a new structured MHA with fewer parameters and lower complexity. Given an input matrix, CSP circularly shifts the samples of different channels with various steps and then sorts grouped samples of each channel. This operator is equivalent to implicitly implementing cross-channel attention maps as permutation matrices, which achieves linear complexity and suppresses the risk of rank collapse when representing data. We replace the MHA of some representative models with CSP and test the CSP-based models in several discriminative tasks, including image classification and long sequence analysis. Experiments show that the CSP-based models achieve comparable or better performance with fewer parameters and lower computational costs than the classic Transformer and its state-of-the-art variants. The code is available at https://github.com/DaShenZi721/CSP.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes CSP (Channel-wise Sample Permutation), which replaces the standard softmax-based multi-head attention with permutation matrices (circular shifting + group sorting operations). Instead of computing weighted averages of value vectors (which causes the reduced effective resolution problem), CSP applies hard permutations to reorder samples across channels. This eliminates the attention averaging issue entirely because permutation matrices are sparse doubly stochastic matrices with all-one spectrums, avoiding the rank collapse that arises from averaging. The paper proves theoretically that CSP suppresses rank collapse (linear convergence rate vs. doubly exponential for standard MHA) and demonstrates empirically that CSP-based models achieve competitive or better performance with fewer parameters and lower complexity.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap for discriminative tasks (classification, long sequence analysis). However, the authors explicitly note a limitation: CSP is designed for doubly stochastic attention maps, which restricts its application to generative tasks where attention maps are lower-triangular (causal masking). For generative/decoder-based Transformers, imposing doubly stochastic constraints would result in trivial identity matrices, so the effective resolution problem from attention averaging in causal self-attention remains open. Additionally, the paper does not analyze whether the "effective resolution" issue (as distinct from rank collapse) is fully resolved in all architectural configurations.
evidence_snippets: This operator is equivalent to implicitly implementing cross-channel attention maps as permutation matrices, which achieves linear complexity and suppresses the risk of rank collapse when representing data.

Applying CSP can suppress this risk, which is supported by the following theorem. ... Theorem 1 indicates a linear convergence rate of the residual. It means that the model applying CSP avoids the rapid decay of the matrix rank.

The spectrums achieved by the circular shifting and CSP operators decay much more slowly than the spectrum achieved by MHA. This observed phenomenon serves as a strong validation of the theoretical result in Theorem 1, providing further evidence that the representation model using permutation-based attention maps indeed carries a lower risk of rank collapse compared to the classic MHA-based model.

paper.title: Primal-Attention: Self-attention through Asymmetric Kernel SVD in Primal Representation
paper.abstract: Recently, a new line of works has emerged to understand and improve self-attention in Transformers by treating it as a kernel machine. However, existing works apply the methods for symmetric kernels to the asymmetric self-attention, resulting in a nontrivial gap between the analytical understanding and numerical implementation. In this paper, we provide a new perspective to represent and optimize self-attention through asymmetric Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD), which is also motivated by the low-rank property of self-attention normally observed in deep layers. Through asymmetric KSVD, $i$) a primal-dual representation of self-attention is formulated, where the optimization objective is cast to maximize the projection variances in the attention outputs; $ii$) a novel attention mechanism, i.e., Primal-Attention, is proposed via the primal representation of KSVD, avoiding explicit computation of the kernel matrix in the dual; $iii$) with KKT conditions, we prove that the stationary solution to the KSVD optimization in Primal-Attention yields a zero-value objective. In this manner, KSVD optimization can be implemented by simply minimizing a regularization loss, so that low-rank property is promoted without extra decomposition. Numerical experiments show state-of-the-art performance of our Primal-Attention with improved efficiency. Moreover, we demonstrate that the deployed KSVD optimization regularizes Primal-Attention with a sharper singular value decay than that of the canonical self-attention, further verifying the great potential of our method. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that provides a primal-dual representation for the asymmetric kernel in self-attention and successfully applies it to modeling and optimization.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes Primal-Attention, a reformulation of self-attention through asymmetric Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD). It provides a primal-dual representation of self-attention, avoids explicit kernel matrix computation, and uses a regularization loss to promote low-rank properties. The paper achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks with improved efficiency. However, its focus is on addressing the asymmetry gap in kernel-based interpretations of self-attention and on promoting low-rank structure, not on the problem of reduced effective resolution from attention averaging.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap of "reduced effective resolution from attention averaging" at all. The gap concerns the fact that self-attention weights are averaged over positions, which reduces effective resolution — a problem that Multi-Head Attention is designed to counteract. This paper does not discuss, analyze, or propose solutions for this resolution-averaging problem. Instead, it focuses on a different issue: the asymmetry between symmetric kernel methods used in prior work and the inherently asymmetric nature of self-attention kernels. The paper's proposed solution (Primal-Attention via KSVD) is about low-rank regularization and efficient computation, not about preserving or improving effective resolution that is lost through averaging.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is well-scoped (causal attention only) and evaluable (rank/variance metrics + downstream task performance). CSP provides a strong methodological starting point for the bidirectional case, and the problem is a natural extension. Data and compute are moderate — standard transformer training on text data suffices; no frontier-scale models required. The main difficulty is genuinely mathematical: CSP's hard permutations rely on doubly-stochastic structure (symmetric), which is fundamentally incompatible with causal/lower-triangular constraints. A solution likely needs a different non-averaging mechanism for the causal setting, not a simple adaptation of CSP. This is a non-trivial algorithmic challenge — feasible for a skilled researcher but requiring genuine insight, placing it at moderate tractability (~0.55).
